# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–26 (Complete – Updated 191)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Autumn in continental Europe, seventh year after Waterloo**. John Sedley deceased (died peacefully in sleep; buried at Brompton churchyard beside wife). Mr. Osborne deceased (died four days after stroke; found at foot of dressing-table). Major Dobbin appointed executor of Osborne's will. Rawdon governs Coventry Island. Georgy established as heir. **Continental tour progressing**: Amelia, Georgy, Jos, and Major Dobbin on steamship and carriage tour; landed Rotterdam, traveled to Cologne, now in Pumpernickel (a small German principality).
- **Key temporal markers**: Chapter 26 opens "summer of seventh year," now extends into autumn as tour continues through continental Europe; narrator traveling in same region, encountered them at various points including theatre in Pumpernickel.
- **Major locations**: London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Gaunt House, Regent Club, Knightsbridge Barracks, Russell Square, Brompton, Conduit Street, Hart Street Bloomsbury, Southampton Row, Kensington Gardens, Camberwell, Slaughters' Inn, Haymarket Theatre, Gillespie Street); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate; Piccadilly; Madras; St. Helena; Cape; Southampton; Staveton (harbor town); Belgium (Brussels, Mount St. John); Bengal; Salford; Regent's Park; Richmond (Star and Garter); Gulton; Harrowgate; Hill farms; Roehampton; Hampton Court; Calcutta; Jamaica; **Rotterdam; Cologne; Free City of Judenstadt; Rhine region; Rhineland; Pumpernickel (small German principality with Court, theatre, Duke's schloss); Mirecombe (village with hill farms); Dunholt (village)**.

## John Sedley's Final Illness and Death (Chapter 26)
**Nursing and Reconciliation**: Amelia nursed father devotedly during final illness; her "sole business of her life" to tend him. Old Sedley, "touched by her love and goodness," forgave past grievances. One night made confession: "Oh, Emmy, I've been thinking we were very unkind and unjust to you." Amelia knelt and prayed by his bedside.

**Death**: Died peacefully in sleep. Buried at Brompton churchyard beside wife. Major Dobbin, Jos, and Georgy followed remains to grave in black cloth coach. Jos returned to Star and Garter at Richmond. Amelia remained, "bowed down by no especial grief," prayed for calm, painless death like father's.

## Mr. Osborne's Stroke and Death (Chapter 26)
**Mental Change and Reconciliation Dinner**: Osborne's mind visibly changing. Asked Georgy about Jos; laughed at boy's imitations. Told Miss Osborne to leave card upon Sedley—"There's no quarrel betwigst me and him anyhow." Card returned; Jos and Dobbin invited to "most splendid and stupid" dinner. Every inch of family plate exhibited. Sedley took down Miss O. to dinner; she was gracious. Dobbin sat apart, timid, by Osborne's side.

**Dobbin's Advocacy**: Osborne asked Major repeatedly about Mrs. George Osborne. Dobbin spoke eloquently of her sufferings, passionate attachment to husband's memory, tender duty to parents, sacrifice of boy. Told Osborne: "You don't know what she endured, sir...If she took your son away from you, she gave hers to you; and however much you loved your George, depend on it, she loved hers ten times more." Osborne replied: "By God, you are a good feller, sir."

**Prevention by Death**: Reconciliation meeting never took place. Old Sedley's lingering illness intervened. Osborne "much shaken of late, and aged," had sent for lawyers and likely "changed something in his will." Found in dressing-room at foot of dressing-table in fit. Doctors sent; Georgy stayed from school. Osborne partially regained consciousness but never spoke again. Died in four days. Pocket of dressing-gown contained letter with great red seal George had written from Waterloo and key to box of son's papers; seals broken—likely read night before seizure while reading great red family Bible in study.

## Mr. Osborne's Will (Chapter 26)
**Terms**: Half property left to George Osborne (minor); remainder between two sisters. Mr. Bullock to continue commercial house affairs. **Annuity**: Five hundred pounds, chargeable on George's property, left to Amelia, "the widow of my beloved son, George Osborne," who was to resume guardianship of boy.

**Dobbin's Provision**: Major William Dobbin appointed executor, named "my beloved son's friend." Will stated he maintained grandson and widow "when they were otherwise without means of support" and bequeathed sum "sufficient to purchase his commission as a Lieutenant-Colonel, or to be disposed of in any way he may think fit."

**Osborne's Intent**: Will showed "the hatred which he had so long cherished had gone out of his heart."

## Amelia's Transformation and New Life (Chapter 26)
**Upon Learning of Reconciliation and Osborne's Support**: When learned William's bounty supported her in poverty, that William gave her husband and son—"oh, then she sank on her knees, and prayed for blessings on that constant and kind heart; she bowed down and humbled herself, and kissed the feet, as it were, of that beautiful and generous affection."

**Visiting Gaunt House**: Clad in deep sables, visited deserted mansion. Found straw littered in front, great blank rooms bearing marks where pictures and mirrors hung. Went to George's upper room. At open window (where she once gazed as child when first taken from her), looked out over Russell Square toward old house where she was born and passed happy days of youth. "They all came back to her, the pleasant holidays, the kind faces, the careless, joyful past times, and the long pains and trials that had since cast her down." She thought of man who had been her "constant protector, her good genius, her sole benefactor, her tender and generous friend."

**New Household and Recognition of Dobbin's Worth**: Took temporary house at Richmond. Major Dobbin had room there, rode over frequently on business behalf of his little ward. During continental tour, discovered Dobbin's true gentlemanly character—generous aims, constant truth, elevated degree, lack of meanness making him simple, honest face, warm and humble heart. "Emmy, in this happy time, found that hers underwent a very great change in respect of the merits of the Major."

## Continental Tour Details (Chapter 26)
**Rhine Journey and Ship Travel**: Party aboard ship at Staveton. Kirsch (courier/interpreter) bellowing polyglot instructions, boasting carriage belonged to "a Nabob from Calcutta and Jamaica enormously rich." Party landed Rotterdam, traveled by steamer to Cologne.

**Jos's Continental Pretensions**: Jos announced arrival in Cologne newspapers as "Herr Graf Lord von Sedley nebst Begleitung aus London." Had court dress; insisted Dobbin bring regimental paraphernalia; announced intention to be presented at foreign courts. Left own card and Major's on "Our Minister" wherever party stopped. Kept journal noting defects or excellences of inns and wines. Did not much engage in afternoon excursions; slept good deal after dinner or basked in arbours. Still fascinated by nobility—observed Earl of Bareacres and family on ship; both "looked rather younger" than remembered from Brussels in '15, with Lady's dark hair now "a beautiful golden auburn" and Lord's red whiskers now "of a rich black with purple and green reflections."

**Amelia's Happiness**: Very happy and pleased. Dobbin carried her stool and sketch-book, admired her drawings. She sat upon steamers' decks and drew crags and castles, or mounted upon donkeys to ascend ancient robber-towers, attended by Georgy and Dobbin. She laughed at Major's droll figure on donkey-back with long legs touching ground. He was party's interpreter; had good military knowledge of German language; he and Georgy fought campaigns of Rhine and Palatinate. "Perhaps it was the happiest time of both their lives...this couple were very decently contented, and enjoyed as pleasant a summer tour as any pair that left England that year."

## Pumpernickel Arrival and Society (Chapter 26)
**Theatre and British Recognition**: Party attended theatre in Pumpernickel. Upon "burst of that beloved and well-known music," every Englishman in house proclaimed membership in British nation—"Sir John and Lady Bullminster (who had taken a house at Pumpernickel for the education of their nine children), the fat gentleman with the mustachios, the long Major in white duck trousers, and the lady with the little boy." Tapeworm, Charge d'Affaires (nephew and heir of old Marshal Tiptoff, now deceased, who was General Tiptoff before Waterloo, Colonel of --th regiment in which Major Dobbin served; died this year after aspic of plovers' eggs; regiment given by His Majesty to Colonel Sir Michael O'Dowd, K.C.B.), rose in his box and bowed.

**Tapeworm's Attentions**: Near end of performance, Tapeworm approached Jos with "fascinating smile" and invitation to stay in Pumpernickel: "It is a dull place, but we want some nice people, and we would try and make it SO agreeable to you." Promised to call next day at inn. "My lord nearly sent Jos off his legs...with a Parthian grin and glance which he thought must finish Mrs. Osborne completely."

**Post-Theatre Departure**: After performance, Duchess Dowager departed in "jingling old coach" attended by two old maids of honour and spindle-shanked gentleman in waiting. Duke and Transparent family departed with great officers of state amid saluting guards and flaring torches of running footmen in scarlet. English party came out—boy yawning, Major taking great pains keeping shawl over Mrs. Osborne's head, Jos looking grand with crush opera-hat and hand in voluminous white waistcoat. Narrator and companions took off hats to acquaintances; lady presented "little smile and curtsey." Jos walked and smoked cigar homeward; other three took carriage from inn under Kirsch's superintendence.

**Lodging and Social Advancement**: Narrator's group walked with Jos, who praised Pumpernickel's agrémens—shooting-parties, battues, balls and entertainments at hospitable Court, good society, excellent theatre, cheap living. Jos spoke of "our Minister" as "most delightful and affable person." Jos creaked up stairs to bedward, followed by Kirsch with flambeau. Narrator's group "rather hoped that nice-looking woman would be induced to stay some time in the town."

**Tapeworm's Visit and Court Introduction**: Tapeworm accepted Jos's invitation to lodge at his quarters. Put dexterous questions to Jos about India and dancing-girls; asked Amelia about "that beautiful boy" (Georgy); complimented her upon "prodigious sensation which she had made in the house"; tried to fascinate Dobbin talking of late war and Pumpernickel contingent exploits under Hereditary Prince, now Duke.

**Dr. Glauber's Scheme**: Doctor von Glauber, Body Physician to H.S.H. the Duke, speedily convinced Jos that Pumpernickel mineral springs and Doctor's particular treatment would "infallibly restore the Bengalee to youth and slimness." Boasted: "Dere came here last year Sheneral Bulkeley, an English Sheneral, tvice so pic as you, sir. I sent him back qvite tin after tree months, and he danced vid Baroness Glauber at the end of two."

**Commitment to Stay**: Jos's mind made up; springs, Doctor, Court, and Charge d'Affaires convinced him. He proposed to spend autumn in Pumpernickel. Next day, Tapeworm presented Jos and Major to Victor Aurelius XVII (the sovereign), conducted by Count de Schlusselback, Marshal of the Court. Straightway invited to dinner at Court. Upon announcement of intention to stay, "politest ladies of the whole town instantly called upon Mrs. Osborne"; as not one was under rank of Baroness, "Jos's delight was beyond expression." Wrote to Chutney at Club that Service highly appreciated in Germany, intended to show Count de Schlusselback how to stick pig in Indian fashion, and that "august friends, the Duke and Duchess, were everything that was kind and civil."

## Georgy Osborne (Chapter 26)
**Character and Education**: Now eleven years old; boy's "quick brain" revealed grandfather "a dullard." Day boy at Reverend Lawrence Veal's School (Hart Street, Bloomsbury). Marked aristos in Greek, optimus in Latin, très bien in French. Schoolboys call Veal "Longtail."

**On Continental Tour**: Present at plays but walked ahead during excursions, climbing towers and trees, while Amelia and Dobbin walked soberly below. Made "prodigious advance in the knowledge of High Dutch" by conversing with Herr Kirsch on carriage box; could talk to hotel waiters and postilions in way that charmed his mother and amused his guardian. Yawning drearily at theatre in Pumpernickel.

**Inheritance**: Now heir to half Osborne's substantial property. Will restored him to mother's guardianship. Boy remained active, imperious, good-natured.

## Reconciliation with Mrs. Frederick Bullock (Chapter 26)
Mrs. Frederick Bullock, "although despoiled by that little monster of one-half of the sum which she expected from her father, nevertheless showed her charitableness of spirit by being reconciled to the mother and the boy." One day chariot with golden bullocks emblazoned on panels drove to Amelia's house. Bullock family "made an irruption into the garden, where Amelia was reading a book, Jos was in an arbour placidly dipping strawberries into wine, and the Major in one of his Indian jackets was giving a back to Georgy, who chose to jump over him." Those ladies met "after an absence of more than fifteen years. During Emmy's cares and poverty the other had never once thought about coming to see her, but now that she was decently prosperous in the world, her sister-in-law came to her as a matter of course."

**Bullock's Scheming (rumor)**: Per Rowdy and Hollyock's conversation, Mrs. Bullock "is always scheming and managing. She wants Mrs. Osborne's account to be taken from our house to hers--and the way in which she coaxes that boy and makes him sit by that blear-eyed little Rosa is perfectly ridiculous."

## Miss Swartz's Renewed Friendship (Chapter 26)
Old friend Miss Swartz and her husband came "thundering over from Hampton Court, with flaming yellow liveries, and was as impetuously fond of Amelia as ever. Miss Swartz would have liked her always if she could have seen her. One must do her that justice. But, que voulez vous?--in this vast town one has not the time to go and seek one's friends; if they drop out of the rank they disappear, and we march on without them."

## Rawdon Crawley (Chapter 23–24)
Governor of Coventry Island, three thousand per year. Complete moral transformation: maintains honor, fulfills obligations, provides for son's education, compensates those wronged. Separated from Rebecca permanently after duel with Steyne.

## Rebecca's Fate (Chapter 24)
Bailiffs seized Curzon Street property. Rawdon made her "tolerable annuity." Whereabouts unknown; "Who cared!"
